title: RTP, codecs, and DTMF
summary: RTP headers, payload types, codec documents, RTCP, telephone-event, packet time, and one-way audio.

lessons.title: The RTP header
lessons.summary: RTP version 2 carries a sequence number, a timestamp, an SSRC, and a marker bit. SIP does not carry those fields.
objectives: Name version, sequence, timestamp, SSRC, and marker
Separate the RTP header from the SIP message
Use the timestamp clock of the payload, not the wall clock

illustration.title: Fixed RTP header
illustration.caption: Version 2 is the version you will capture. The marker bit is part of this header.

sections.h: Version 2 and the fields beside it
paragraphs: RFC 3550 defines RTP, and the version field in the header is 2. The same header carries a marker bit, a 7-bit payload type, a 16-bit sequence number, a 32-bit timestamp, and a 32-bit SSRC.

The sequence number increases by one for each RTP packet that source sends, so a gap is a loss signal. The SSRC is chosen by the sender and identifies that source inside the session, which is a different job from the SIP Call-ID.

sections.h: The timestamp is a media clock
paragraphs: The timestamp advances by the number of clock ticks in the packet, using the payload clock, and it is not a wall-clock time. For 20 ms of G.711 at 8000 Hz the timestamp increases by 160, and the same step of 160 applies to G.722 because its rtpmap clock is also 8000.

For audio, the marker bit is set on the first packet after a silence gap, which is an RFC 3551 use of the bit RFC 3550 defined. A 200 OK never contains these fields, so a media fault is read from the RTP capture.

fault.symptom: The 200 OK is present, audio is choppy, and the ticket asks for the SIP CSeq to explain missing words.

choices: The gap is in the RTP sequence, which SIP CSeq does not report

fault.why: RFC 3550 sequence numbers live on RTP packets. A jump from 44011 to 44014 is media loss.
fault.cause: The troubleshooting notes treated CSeq as the media sequence.
fault.fix: Capture the RTP ports from SDP and read version, sequence, timestamp, SSRC, and marker there. Use RTCP for a loss summary.

lessons.title: Static and dynamic payload types
lessons.summary: RFC 3551 assigns static payload types. Dynamic types are named by rtpmap, and G.722 stays at clock 8000.
objectives: List static types 0, 8, 9, and 18 with their clocks
Require rtpmap for payload types 96 through 127
Refuse a G.722 clock of 16000

illustration.title: Static types you must not renumber
illustration.caption: Dynamic types 96 through 127 take their meaning from rtpmap on that m-line only.

paragraphs: RFC 3551 assigns a small set of static payload types, including 0 PCMU/8000, 8 PCMA/8000, 9 G722/8000, and 18 G729/8000. Those numbers mean those encodings even when the offer omits rtpmap, and they are not free to reuse for opus or telephone-event.
PCMU and PCMA are both G.711, and they are not the same encoding. A peer that offers only payload 0 will not decode payload 8, so the answer has to pick a type both sides listed.

sections.h: Dynamic types and the G.722 clock
paragraphs: Payload types 96 through 127 are dynamic, and they match only through the rtpmap encoding name, which is why two gateways can use different numbers for one codec. A policy that equates those numbers across vendors will select the wrong encoding or select nothing.

G.722 keeps rtpmap clock 8000 while the audio sample rate is 16 kHz. A 20 ms packet still advances the RTP timestamp by 160. An offer that says G722/16000 does not match an implementation that followed RFC 3551.

lessons.title: G.711, G.729, and Opus
lessons.summary: Choose a codec both sides named. Read RFC 6716 and the Opus license before you draw any legal conclusion.
objectives: Separate G.711 PCMU from PCMA
Point at ITU-T G.729 without stating a patent date
Read the Opus RFC and the license, and stop there

illustration.title: What to read before you pick
illustration.caption: Codec documents and license pages are different from the payload type number.
rows: RFC 6716, the Opus license, IETF IPR
opus, clock from the payload format

paragraphs: G.711 is the ITU-T recommendation behind PCMU and PCMA, both at an RTP clock of 8000 and a payload rate of 64 kbit/s. They interoperate only when the offer and the answer select the same one, mu-law or A-law.

G.729 is the ITU-T recommendation named by rtpmap as G729/8000, static payload type 18, and you read that recommendation before you deploy it. This course does not state a patent date or a licensing result for G.729.

sections.h: Opus, the RFC, and the license
paragraphs: Opus is specified in RFC 6716, and offers name it with an rtpmap encoding of opus, commonly opus/48000/2. The payload type number is dynamic, so the match is still the encoding name and not a fixed number.
Read RFC 6716 and the Opus license, and check the IETF IPR disclosures, before you decide what the license allows. This lesson stops at that reading and does not state a further legal conclusion.

lessons.title: RTCP sender and receiver reports
lessons.summary: RTCP sender reports and receiver reports describe the RTP flow. A SIP 200 OK does not report loss.
objectives: Distinguish sender reports from receiver reports
Look in RTCP for loss and jitter
Pair RTCP with the RTP port using the RFC 3550 default

illustration.title: What a report is for
illustration.caption: RFC 3550 pairs RTCP with RTP. SIP status codes are not a substitute.
rows: The participant has been sending RTP
Packet count, octet count, NTP and RTP timestamps

paragraphs: RFC 3550 defines RTCP sender reports and receiver reports. A sender report is used when that participant has recently sent RTP, and it includes sender packet and octet counts plus reception reports.
A receiver report carries reception reports without that sender block. Fraction lost, cumulative packets lost, and interarrival jitter are how you see damage that a SIP 200 OK will never mention.
RFC 3550 says RTP should use an even port and RTCP the next higher port. When you capture media, open that pair before you declare the call healthy.
One-way RTP often shows a sender report from only one side. Combine that fact with the SDP direction and the c= address, and use the Wireshark RTP display-filter reference when you slice the capture.

lessons.title: telephone-event and other digit paths
lessons.summary: telephone-event is RFC 4733, a dynamic payload. Events 0 through 15 are DTMF. INFO and KPML are different tools.
objectives: Negotiate telephone-event in SDP by encoding name
Limit DTMF events to 0 through 15
Keep SIP INFO and KPML separate from RFC 4733

illustration.title: Three digit paths
illustration.caption: Only telephone-event is RTP. The others are signaling, and one of them is not an IETF body.
rows: Dynamic RTP payload. Events 0-15 are DTMF
A SIP method. Not the DTMF codec
SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY for key presses

paragraphs: RFC 4733 defines telephone-event, and it obsoletes RFC 2833. The RFC Editor status banner is the authority for that status. The encoding is negotiated in SDP as a dynamic payload type, so you match the rtpmap name telephone-event and you do not insist on one global payload type number.

Events 0 through 15 are the DTMF events. Event 16 is flash, so a fmtp range of 0-15 is the DTMF set and a range of 0-16 adds flash. The telephone-event clock follows the audio, commonly 8000 with G.711.
SIP INFO is specified in RFC 6086 as a mid-dialog method for application information, and it is not telephone-event. Seeing INFO on a call does not mean RFC 4733 was negotiated.

A body of application/dtmf-relay is a vendor body, not an IETF standard. Recognize it in a trace and do not describe it as the standards-track DTMF encoding. KPML, RFC 4730, is a third path that uses SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY when an application wants digits in signaling.

lessons.title: ptime, packet rate, and EF
lessons.summary: ptime is SDP. Twenty milliseconds of G.711 is 50 packets per second and 160 bytes of payload, plus headers. Voice sits in the EF class.
objectives: Read a=ptime as milliseconds of media per packet
Compute the G.711 20 ms packet rate and payload size
Place voice in EF using RFC 4594 and RFC 3246, without a router config

illustration.title: 20 ms G.711
illustration.caption: Payload math is not a router configuration. EF is the service class, defined elsewhere.

paragraphs: a=ptime gives the packetization time in milliseconds for that media stream. It is SDP, so it is negotiated in the offer and the answer, and it is not an RTP header field and not a SIP method.

Twenty milliseconds of G.711 is 50 packets per second. Each packet carries 160 bytes of payload, because 8000 samples per second times 0.020 seconds is 160 eight-bit samples, which is a 64 kbit/s payload. IP, UDP, and RTP headers sit on top of those 160 bytes.

sections.h: Voice is in the EF class
paragraphs: RFC 4594 places voice in the Expedited Forwarding class, and RFC 3246 defines that per-hop behavior. Cite both when you say why voice is marked EF, and keep the marking decision in the operator's QoS design.
This lesson does not include a router configuration. ptime still changes the packet rate the marker has to carry: 20 ms is 50 packets per second, and a longer ptime sends fewer, larger packets.

lessons.title: One-way audio
lessons.summary: A 200 OK can be perfect while one RTP direction is missing. Read direction, c=, and who is actually sending.
objectives: Separate a completed offer/answer from flowing RTP
Check sendonly, recvonly, and inactive before blaming the codec
Use RTCP to see which side is silent

illustration.title: What to check, in order
illustration.caption: Signaling success is the first box, not the last.

sections.h: Signaling can be done while one direction is not
paragraphs: One-way audio means RTP is arriving in one direction and not in the other. The SIP 200 OK only proves that an answer was delivered, so the next read is the direction attribute on each m-line.

An answer of sendonly means that answerer will send and does not want to receive. An answer of inactive means neither side sends. Either one produces a missing direction even when the codec name matched.

If both directions are sendrecv and RTP still fails one way, compare the c= address and the m= port with the UDP packets you captured. The address in SDP is where the sender was told to transmit, and a packet that never arrives there is a path problem.

RTCP sender reports show which side has sent. Filter the capture with the Wireshark RTP display filters, and use the SIP display-filter reference for the signaling half. Do not change payload types until direction and path have been read.
